claims.text: Dispersing graphene within the Cu phase will increase the overall thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite.
Dispersing graphene within the Cu phase will not compromise the mechanical durability of a W–Cu composite.
Dispersing graphene within the Cu phase will not compromise the irradiation resistance of a W–Cu composite.
Graphene or reduced graphene oxide should be introduced as a uniform dispersion in the Cu matrix during composite processing.
Suitable processing will allow graphene to form continuous thermal-conduction pathways at Cu grain boundaries.
High thermal flux and radiation are typical operating conditions for fusion-reactor environments.
The intervention will produce graphene networks at Cu interfaces within the composite.
Graphene has exceptionally high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Integrated graphene will form additional heat-transfer bridges between Cu grains.
The graphene heat-transfer bridges will enable more efficient phonon transport.
Controlled graphene integration will preserve mechanical interlocking between W and Cu.
Controlled graphene integration will not introduce significant defects that lower irradiation resistance.
The graphene-reinforced composite may exhibit an approximately 10–20% increase in thermal conductivity relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite.
The graphene-reinforced composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the baseline W–Cu composite.
The graphene-reinforced composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the baseline W–Cu composite.
Graphene aggregation or graphene-associated interfacial defects may prevent the predicted benefits.
The predicted benefits require a processing route that does not adversely alter the composite's primary microstructure.
The thermal-conductivity improvement and long-term stability of graphene interfaces under irradiation may vary with manufacturing conditions.
